A new, more intuitive training system for excavator operators has been unveiled by a leading construction technology firm, promising to shorten the learning curve for heavy‑equipment operators. The platform combines interactive simulations with real‑time feedback, allowing trainees to practice complex manoeuvres in a virtual environment that closely mimics on‑site conditions. Early trials conducted at the company’s test facility indicate that operators can reach proficiency in a fraction of the time required by traditional classroom and field‑based programs.

The system’s design incorporates adaptive learning algorithms that identify individual skill gaps and tailor exercises accordingly, reducing the need for repetitive drills. In addition, the software records performance metrics that can be reviewed by instructors, ensuring that safety protocols are consistently met. Industry analysts suggest that faster training cycles could lower labor costs and increase equipment utilization, while also addressing the growing shortage of qualified heavy‑equipment operators in the construction sector.

If the projected efficiencies materialize, the new training solution could become a standard component of operator certification programs across North America and beyond. The company plans to roll out the system to its partner sites over the next six months, with a broader market launch slated for early 2027.
author: MIT News

title: North Korea says scaling back US‑South Korea drills changes nothing
content:
Washington faced sharp criticism on Tuesday after the Trump administration announced a sudden suspension of the annual joint military exercises with South Korea, a cornerstone of the U.S.–South Korean security alliance. The decision, made without prior consultation with Seoul, was presented by the White House as a confidence‑building measure aimed at easing regional tensions amid ongoing diplomatic outreach to North Korea. The planned drills, which typically involve thousands of troops and a range of live‑fire and amphibious operations, were slated to begin later this month and have been conducted regularly for decades as a deterrent against Pyongyang’s missile program.

U.S. lawmakers, defense analysts and South Korean officials denounced the pull‑back, arguing that it signals a retreat from alliance commitments and could erode American credibility on the global stage. Critics emphasized that the abrupt change undermines the deterrent posture that has underpinned stability in the Korean Peninsula and may embolden North Korea’s aggressive behavior. The administration, while maintaining that the move is temporary and part of a broader diplomatic strategy, faces pressure to reassure allies that the United States remains steadfast in its security guarantees.
author: Euronews

title: Trump threatens economic sanctions on countries aiding Iran
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump warned on Tuesday that any nation that assists or conducts business with Iran will face what he called an “economic D‑Day,” signaling a potential escalation of American sanctions against Tehran’s allies. The remark was made during a press briefing at the White House, where the president reiterated his administration’s stance that Iran’s nuclear program and regional activities pose a direct threat to U.S. interests and that the United States will not tolerate external support that could bolster the Iranian economy.

The statement follows a series of executive orders and legislative measures aimed at tightening financial restrictions on Iran, including secondary sanctions that target non‑U.S. entities engaging in prohibited transactions. Treasury officials have indicated that the “economic D‑Day” threat could translate into expanded asset freezes, prohibitions on access to the U.S. financial system, and heightened enforcement actions against foreign firms. International partners have expressed concern over the possible impact on global trade and diplomatic relations, while the administration maintains that the policy is intended to pressure Iran into compliance with nuclear agreements and curb its regional influence.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Saarland University team to study metallic‑glass alloys on ISS with levitating droplets
content:
Researchers from Saarland University, led by materials scientist Ralf Busch, are preparing for their first science‑in‑space mission. Beginning 31 August, the team will conduct a one‑week remote investigation of metallic‑glass alloys aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The experiments will focus on the behavior of hot, levitating droplets of the alloys, allowing scientists to observe their properties without the influence of Earth’s gravity.

The project is a collaboration with the European Space Agency (ESA) and the German Aerospace Center (DLR). By using the ISS’s microgravity environment, the researchers aim to gain new insights into the fundamental characteristics of metallic glasses, which could inform the development of advanced materials for aerospace, automotive, and industrial applications. The data collected will be transmitted to the team on the ground for real‑time analysis and subsequent publication.

If the mission proceeds as planned, the findings will represent a significant step forward in space‑based materials science. The results are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of how metallic glasses behave under extreme thermal and microgravity conditions, potentially leading to the design of stronger, more resilient materials for future technologies.
author: Phys.org

title: NASA Swift Telescope Rescue Mission Fails, Satellite to Re-enter Earth
content:
NASA announced on Wednesday that its $30 million attempt to rescue the Swift space telescope has failed, as the rescue spacecraft could not be controlled during the mission. Swift, a NASA observatory that monitors gamma‑ray bursts, was slated to be moved into a higher orbit by a robotic vehicle in an unprecedented effort to extend its operational life.

The rescue plan involved docking a robotic spacecraft to Swift and then using it to boost the telescope into a safer, more stable orbit. However, the robotic vehicle lost control before it could complete the maneuver, rendering the rescue attempt impossible. With no viable means to keep Swift aloft, mission planners have now concluded that the satellite will re‑enter Earth’s atmosphere and is expected to disintegrate later this year.

The loss of Swift marks the end of a key instrument for high‑energy astrophysics, but the mission’s outcome will inform future rescue attempts of aging spacecraft. NASA will continue to monitor the re‑entry trajectory to ensure any debris poses no risk to populated areas.
author: France 24

title: Prince Harry and Meghan to return to UK after six years in US
content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are set to return to the United Kingdom after more than six years of residence in the United States, according to recent reports. The couple, who stepped back from senior royal duties in 2020 and relocated to California, are expected to settle in a private home in the UK as they prepare to resume a more public life.

Sources say the former senior royals will not be moving into a palace or official residence but will instead live in a private property. The decision follows a period of relative seclusion in the U.S. and aligns with the couple’s stated intention to re‑engage with the British public and charitable work. The move is being managed by the royal household and is expected to be completed in the coming weeks.

The return marks a significant shift for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who have previously focused on independent projects and media ventures abroad. Their homecoming will be closely watched by the media and the public as they transition back into a life that, while still private, will involve renewed engagement with the United Kingdom’s social and charitable institutions.
author: DW World

title: Russian strike on Kyiv kills three, injures twenty
content:
At least 14 of the 20 individuals injured in a recent strike on Kyiv have been admitted to hospitals, Ukrainian officials confirmed on Sunday. The attack, which took place in the capital’s central district during the early evening hours, left a mixture of civilians and emergency responders wounded, prompting a swift medical response from city hospitals and first‑aid teams.

Health authorities said the majority of the victims are receiving treatment for shrapnel injuries and blast‑related trauma, while the remaining six injured persons are being monitored on an outpatient basis. Local law enforcement and emergency services are continuing investigations into the source of the strike, and security officials have urged residents to remain vigilant as the situation is assessed.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Former Liberian Vice President Charged in Drug Trafficking Probe
content:
Former West Palm Beach mayor Jewel Howard‑Taylor has been indicted on federal charges that allege she illegally facilitated the importation and distribution of controlled substances and engaged in a money‑laundering scheme to conceal the proceeds. The indictment, unsealed by a U.S. District Court in Miami, accuses Howard‑Taylor of acting as an intermediary for a network that moved narcotics into Florida and then used a series of shell companies and offshore accounts to disguise the illicit revenue.

According to the charging documents, Howard‑Taylor allegedly coordinated with overseas suppliers, arranged shipments through commercial freight channels, and oversaw the sale of the drugs to local distributors. Prosecutors say she also directed the conversion of drug proceeds into legitimate‑looking investments, violating the Bank Secrecy Act and related statutes. Howard‑Taylor has pleaded not guilty and is scheduled to appear for a preliminary hearing next month, after which a trial date will be set. If convicted, she faces significant prison time and forfeiture of assets tied to the alleged scheme.
author: BBC World

title: Brain’s Frontoparietal Cortex Reorganizes in Real Time to Handle Uncertainty
content:
Researchers have uncovered that the brain’s frontoparietal cortex operates with remarkable flexibility when faced with uncertainty and changing circumstances. The study shows that this network does not simply increase its overall activity as tasks become more difficult; instead, it actively reorganizes its communication patterns with other brain regions in real time to access the specific information required for decision making.

Using advanced neuroimaging techniques, scientists observed that the frontoparietal cortex dynamically adjusts its connectivity based on the type of information needed—whether it involves sensory input, memory recall, or strategic planning. This real‑time reconfiguration allows the brain to efficiently allocate resources, ensuring that the most relevant neural pathways are engaged for each decision context.

The findings highlight a sophisticated neural mechanism underlying adaptive cognition, offering new insights into how the brain manages complex, uncertain environments. Understanding this dynamic network could inform future research into cognitive disorders and guide the development of interventions that enhance decision‑making flexibility.
author: Science Daily

title: MIT Physicists Observe Ice‑Like Electron Phase in Quantum Material
content:
MIT physicists have uncovered that two distinct electronic phases can coexist within a single quantum material, each arising through markedly different processes. In one scenario, the phase develops gradually, with electrons transitioning smoothly as external conditions such as temperature or pressure change. In the other, the phase nucleates in isolated pockets that expand outward like growing ice crystals, creating a patchwork of electronic behavior across the material.

The team employed advanced spectroscopic and imaging techniques to track the evolution of these phases at the nanoscale. Their observations suggest that the smooth transition is driven by a continuous change in the electronic band structure, while the crystalline‑like pockets result from localized fluctuations that trigger a first‑order transition in confined regions. By mapping these mechanisms, the researchers provide a clearer picture of how exotic properties—such as superconductivity and magnetism—can emerge and coexist within the same material.

This insight offers a new framework for designing quantum materials with tailored electronic properties. Understanding the distinct pathways that lead to phase formation could guide the development of next‑generation superconductors and spintronic devices, where controlled coexistence of multiple quantum states is essential.
author: Science Daily

title: AI-designed intrabodies offer new treatment possibilities for neurodegenerative diseases
content:
Researchers have announced a novel technique that converts conventional antibodies into miniature, cell‑penetrating molecules capable of targeting disease‑related proteins inside human cells. The approach, developed by a multidisciplinary team of scientists, reengineers the antibody structure to produce small, stable fragments that can cross cellular membranes and bind to intracellular targets that have traditionally been difficult to reach with therapeutic agents.

The new platform has shown promise against a range of neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s disease, and motor neurone disease. By enabling the engineered molecules to interact directly with the misfolded proteins that drive these disorders, the method offers a potential pathway to more effective treatments that can intervene at the molecular level within affected neurons. Early laboratory studies demonstrate that the fragments can reduce toxic protein aggregates and improve cellular viability, suggesting a viable strategy for future drug development.

If the technique can be translated into clinical applications, it could broaden the arsenal of therapeutic options for patients with currently incurable neurodegenerative diseases. Continued research will focus on optimizing delivery, ensuring safety, and evaluating efficacy in animal models before moving toward human trials.
author: Science Daily

title: Turns Are Better Than Radians
content:
A recent article published on ComputerEnhance, titled “Turns are better than radians,” argues that the unit of a full rotation—known as a turn—offers practical advantages over the traditional radian measure for expressing angles. The piece, which has attracted modest attention on the Hacker News forum, received ten points and three comments from readers who engaged with its technical claims.

The author outlines several reasons for preferring turns: they map directly to fractions of a circle, eliminating the need for the 2π factor that appears in many trigonometric formulas; they are dimensionless like radians but provide an intuitive sense of proportion, making mental calculations and educational explanations more straightforward. The article cites examples from programming, physics, and engineering where using turns simplifies code and reduces errors, and it notes that some language libraries already support turn‑based constants. While a few commenters raised concerns about compatibility with established mathematical conventions, the overall discussion highlighted a growing interest in re‑examining angle‑measurement standards.
author: Hacker News

title: UN Calls on Israel to Condemn Incitement Over New West Bank Outposts
content:
Reports of new illegal Israeli outposts in the occupied West Bank sparked concern at United Nations headquarters on Wednesday, prompting officials to highlight the potential breach of international law. The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) urged Israel to denounce statements made by its national security minister, which it characterized as incitement to “violence amounting to atrocity crimes” against Palestinians.

In its briefing, the OHCHR reiterated that the establishment of unauthorized settlements contravenes the Fourth Geneva Convention and called for immediate action to prevent further escalation. The agency also requested that Israeli authorities publicly condemn the minister’s rhetoric and take steps to ensure the protection of Palestinian civilians, emphasizing the UN’s broader commitment to upholding human rights standards in the region.
author: UN News

title: Bodycam footage shows deck collapse during Missouri police warrant
content:
A newly released body‑camera video shows a deck collapsing during a warrant‑execution operation in Huntsville, Missouri. The footage, captured by a patrol officer, was posted to the city’s public‑records portal last week and depicts the deck giving way as officers moved through the residence to secure a warrant.

The incident occurred on the evening of March 12, when the Huntsville Police Department was conducting a search of a private property on the basis of a court‑issued warrant. According to the video, the deck’s structural failure caused several officers to fall, though no serious injuries were reported. The city’s deputy chief confirmed that the department is reviewing the footage and will cooperate with state investigators to determine whether the collapse was due to a pre‑existing structural defect or an unforeseen event.

Authorities have not yet released a formal statement regarding the cause of the collapse. The department has pledged to conduct a thorough investigation and to review its safety protocols for warrant operations in structures with potential structural concerns. The incident underscores the risks law‑enforcement officers face during routine search operations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: South Korea alarmed by Trump’s order to cut joint military drills
content:
Seoul expressed alarm on Monday after the United States announced a reduction in the size and scope of joint military drills with South Korea, a move ordered by former President Donald Trump during his final weeks in office. The decision, which cuts back on the annual “Freedom Shield” exercises that have involved thousands of troops and sophisticated weaponry, was presented as an effort to de‑escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula but has been interpreted by South Korean officials as a signal that the United States may be reassessing its security commitments in the region.

South Korean Defense Minister Lee Jong-sup said the change “creates uncertainty” for the alliance that has underpinned regional stability for more than seven decades, and he called for a prompt clarification from Washington on the future of the partnership. Analysts noted that the timing coincides with heightened North Korean missile activity and ongoing diplomatic talks aimed at curbing nuclear proliferation, raising concerns that a perceived weakening of the U.S. presence could embolden Pyongyang. The United States, through the State Department, affirmed that the core security guarantee remains unchanged, but did not specify how the reduced exercises would affect operational readiness.

The episode underscores lingering doubts in Seoul about the reliability of U.S. security assurances, a sentiment that has resurfaced periodically since the alliance’s inception. While diplomatic channels remain open, both governments are expected to negotiate a revised framework for joint training that balances deterrence objectives with the political sensitivities highlighted by the recent order.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Brazilian drug gangs expand into remote Bolivian village, raising security concerns
content:
Fears are mounting in a remote Bolivian village near the border with Brazil as rival Brazilian drug trafficking organizations vie for control of a key smuggling corridor. Residents report increased armed presence and heightened tension after intelligence agencies identified the area as a strategic link between coca‑producing regions in the Andes and distribution networks in the Amazon basin. The village, which relies on subsistence agriculture and limited tourism, has seen a surge in nighttime patrols and sporadic gunfire, prompting local authorities to request additional security assistance from the Bolivian National Police.

Bolivian officials confirmed that joint operations with Brazilian law‑enforcement counterparts are being planned to disrupt the gangs’ attempts to dominate the route, which is believed to facilitate the movement of cocaine and precursor chemicals. While the government has not disclosed specific deployment details, it emphasized a commitment to protect civilian populations and to restore stability to the border region. Community leaders, meanwhile, have called for increased monitoring and humanitarian aid to mitigate the impact of the conflict on the village’s daily life.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Giant whales enter Greenland waters as sea ice melts
content:
Melting sea‑ice in the Arctic has created new open‑water corridors that are drawing large baleen whales into areas previously inaccessible during winter months, researchers reported this week. Satellite imagery and aerial surveys conducted between 2022 and 2024 show a 30 percent reduction in seasonal ice cover across the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, coinciding with a surge in sightings of humpback, fin and blue whales congregating near the ice edge to feed on dense aggregations of krill and small fish. Scientists from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the University of Washington attribute the phenomenon to a “feeding frenzy” triggered by the sudden availability of prey that had been trapped beneath the ice, now exposed as the ice retreats.

The shift in whale distribution is prompting a reassessment of Arctic marine ecosystems, as the influx of top predators may alter food‑web dynamics and affect indigenous communities that rely on traditional hunting grounds. Ongoing monitoring will track the frequency of these feeding events and evaluate long‑term ecological impacts, while also informing management strategies for both wildlife conservation and sustainable fisheries in the rapidly changing polar region.
author: BBC World

title: Weekly type 2 diabetes jab could replace daily injections
content:
Hundreds of thousands of individuals managing type 2 diabetes may soon have access to a new weekly insulin injection designed to replace daily dosing regimens. The development introduces a simplified treatment option aimed at reducing the routine burden of self-administered injections while maintaining established glucose control standards. Health officials and pharmaceutical developers have indicated that the therapy could streamline long-term diabetes management for a substantial portion of the patient population.

Clinical
author: BBC Health

title: Korea Institute of Materials Science creates lead‑free perovskite sensor detecting ammonia at 1 ppm
content:
A team headed by principal researcher Myungkwan Song of the Energy & Environment Materials Research Division at the Korea Institute of Materials Science (KIMS) has announced the creation of an ultrasensitive ammonia gas sensor built from an environmentally friendly, lead‑free perovskite material. The new device promises to detect trace levels of ammonia with unprecedented precision, a capability that could improve safety monitoring in industrial settings, agricultural facilities, and urban air‑quality networks.

The sensor’s core is a lead‑free perovskite crystal that exhibits exceptional electronic conductivity and surface reactivity when exposed to ammonia molecules. By eliminating lead, the material addresses long‑standing toxicity concerns associated with conventional perovskite sensors, while its nanostructured morphology enhances the active surface area and accelerates charge transfer. Early laboratory tests indicate a detection limit in the parts‑per‑billion range, outperforming many current commercial ammonia detectors that typically respond only at parts‑per‑million concentrations.

If the performance can be replicated in field deployments, the technology could offer a low‑cost, high‑accuracy alternative for real‑time monitoring of ammonia emissions from livestock farms, fertilizer storage, and chemical plants. The KIMS team plans to collaborate with industry partners to integrate the sensor into portable monitoring kits and to explore scaling the fabrication process for commercial production.
author: Phys.org

title: Climate Change Alters England's Historic Green and Pleasant Landscape
content:
In 1804, William Blake’s poem *Jerusalem* opened with the line “England’s green and pleasant land,” invoking an idealized pastoral vision that has echoed through the past two centuries. The phrase captures a romanticized image of the English countryside, with its rolling hills and serene pastures, and has become a cultural touchstone that links the nation’s identity to its landscape.

Blake’s depiction of a “green and pleasant” England has influenced literary and artistic representations of the country, reinforcing a narrative that equates national character with natural beauty. Over time, the image has been referenced in political discourse, tourism campaigns, and environmental discussions, underscoring how a poetic description can shape collective memory and public perception of a place.

The enduring resonance of Blake’s vision demonstrates how literary imagery can transcend its original context to become a lasting symbol of national identity. As contemporary writers and historians revisit the poem, the “green and pleasant land” continues to serve as a reference point for discussions about England’s cultural heritage and its relationship to the natural environment.
author: Phys.org

title: WWII Mobilization Shaped Modern Energy and Material Consumption
content:
A recent study published in the *International Journal of Sustainable Development* has traced the origins of today’s resource‑intensive economies back to the mobilization efforts of World War II. The authors examined eight countries that participated in the conflict, including both Allied and Axis powers, and analyzed how wartime production demands accelerated the development of industrial infrastructure and energy systems that would later underpin modern economic growth.

The research links the war‑era surge in manufacturing and logistics to the post‑war period known as the Great Acceleration, a phase marked by rapid increases in global energy consumption, material throughput, and environmental degradation. By comparing wartime production data with subsequent economic indicators, the study demonstrates that the infrastructural and technological foundations laid during the war created a trajectory toward higher consumption patterns that persist in contemporary societies.

These findings underscore the long‑term environmental consequences of large‑scale conflict‑driven industrialization. Understanding the historical roots of current resource use can inform policy discussions on sustainability and highlight the need for deliberate strategies to decouple economic growth from environmental harm.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists Discover Learning and Memory Formation in Model Membranes
content:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) has seen a groundbreaking shift in the science of learning thanks to a decades‑long partnership between two of its senior scientists. The collaboration, rooted in the laboratory’s Department of Energy research agenda, has produced a series of studies that challenge conventional models of how knowledge is acquired and retained.

Over the past twenty years, the researchers have combined expertise in computational neuroscience and high‑performance computing to develop sophisticated simulations of neural plasticity. Their work, published in a number of peer‑reviewed journals, demonstrates that learning can be more accurately described as a dynamic, network‑wide process rather than a series of isolated synaptic changes. The team’s findings have implications for both basic science—offering new insights into memory consolidation—and applied fields such as artificial intelligence, where biologically inspired algorithms are increasingly sought after.

The impact of this research extends beyond academia. DOE funding has enabled the deployment of ORNL’s supercomputing resources to test large‑scale models, and the resulting data sets are now being shared with the broader scientific community. As the collaboration continues, it promises to refine our understanding of learning mechanisms and to inform the development of next‑generation cognitive technologies.
author: Phys.org

title: Dyadic coping linked to lower depression in GI cancer survivors
content:
A recent study published in the *European Journal of Cancer* identifies dyadic coping as a modifiable protective factor for the psychological well‑being of middle‑aged and older survivors of gastrointestinal cancer. Dyadic coping refers to the shared strategies couples use to manage stress, and the research demonstrates that stronger, more coordinated coping efforts between partners are linked to lower levels of anxiety, depression, and post‑traumatic stress symptoms in survivors.

The study followed 312 couples in which one partner had completed treatment for colorectal, pancreatic, or gastric cancer. Using validated questionnaires and longitudinal interviews, researchers measured dyadic coping behaviours and psychological outcomes over a 12‑month period. Results showed that couples who engaged in collaborative problem‑solving, emotional support, and mutual reassurance reported significantly better mental health outcomes than those with less coordinated coping. The authors suggest that interventions aimed at enhancing dyadic coping—such as couple‑based counseling or communication training—could be integrated into survivorship care plans to improve quality of life.

These findings underscore the importance of addressing relational dynamics in cancer survivorship. By fostering stronger partnership coping mechanisms, clinicians may help older patients maintain psychological resilience during the long‑term recovery process. The study calls for further research to develop and test targeted dyadic coping interventions that can be routinely offered to gastrointestinal cancer survivors and their spouses.
author: Phys.org

title: UK to see continued downpours, risk of flash flooding
content:
Heavy, thundery showers have finally broken the UK’s prolonged dry spell, according to meteorologist Ben Rich. The weather service reported that the dry period, which began in late March, has ended as rain has begun to fall across much of England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Rich noted that the showers are continuing into the evening and are expected to persist for the next 24 hours.

Across the country, rainfall totals have reached 15–25 mm in many regions, with some areas in the south‑west and midlands receiving up to 30 mm. The Met Office has issued a moderate‑risk rain warning for several counties, citing the potential for localized flooding and traffic disruptions. The heavy precipitation is also expected to boost reservoir levels and alleviate water shortages that have affected several rural communities.

The end of the dry spell is seen as a relief for farmers and water‑management authorities, who have been grappling with low soil moisture and reduced river flows. While the showers are likely to bring benefits, officials caution that the sudden influx of rain could still pose flood risks, especially in low‑lying urban areas. The Met Office will continue to monitor the situation and update the public on any changes to the weather outlook.
author: BBC Science

title: Study Shows Gradient Descent Can Universally Train Neural Networks
content:
A research manuscript designated arXiv 2007.13664 was uploaded to the pre‑print repository on July 28, 2020. The paper, listed under the arXiv “Computer Science” category, quickly appeared on the technology news aggregator Hacker News, where it received seven up‑votes from the community. No comments were posted on the discussion thread, indicating that while the work attracted a modest level of interest, it did not generate an active debate among readers.

The brief engagement on Hacker News reflects the typical pattern for many scholarly pre‑prints, which are often shared for early visibility and feedback before formal journal publication. As a widely used platform for disseminating scientific findings, arXiv enables researchers to reach a broad audience, while sites like Hacker News provide a venue for rapid, crowd‑sourced appraisal. The modest point total and lack of commentary suggest that the paper has so far drawn limited attention, but its presence on both platforms underscores the growing role of open‑access repositories and online communities in the contemporary research ecosystem.
author: Hacker News

title: NASA cancels rescue mission for Swift gamma-ray observatory
content:
NASA’s Swift Gamma‑Ray Burst Mission is slated to re‑enter Earth’s atmosphere later this year after more than two decades of service. Launched in November 2004, the space telescope has been instrumental in detecting and locating gamma‑ray bursts, providing rapid alerts that have enabled follow‑up observations across the electromagnetic spectrum. With its onboard propellant exhausted and critical systems aging, mission managers have concluded that a controlled de‑orbit is no longer feasible, and the satellite will be allowed to decay naturally.

Officials from the agency’s Flight Operations Directorate confirmed that Swift’s re‑entry trajectory will be monitored closely, and that any surviving fragments are expected to fall over unpopulated oceanic regions, minimizing risk to people or property. The decision reflects standard end‑of‑life procedures for low‑Earth‑orbit assets that have outlived their operational life. Swift’s final descent will mark the end of a mission that contributed more than 1,500 scientific papers and helped shape the modern understanding of high‑energy astrophysical phenomena.
author: Ars Technica

title: Berkeley Professor Admits Using AI to Edit Op‑Ed on Student Math Skills
content:
A San Francisco Standard op‑ed by University of California, Berkeley math professor Zvezdelina Stankova has drawn attention for its use of artificial intelligence in the editing process. Stankova, who has written a 2,000‑word piece last week, disclosed that an AI tool assisted her in refining the article, which criticizes the university system’s “test‑blind” admissions policy. The op‑ed argues that the removal of standardized tests such as the SAT has contributed to a significant gap in foundational math skills among incoming students.

In the article, Stankova claims that some of her students are “five to eight years” behind their peers and lack a basic middle‑school education in fractions and algebra. She attributes this deficiency to the broader admission strategy that prioritizes holistic metrics over traditional test scores. The piece highlights the challenges faced by Berkeley’s mathematics program, noting that students who are not adequately prepared for the rigor of the curriculum are being admitted under the current system.

Stankova’s admission that AI helped edit her op‑ed underscores the growing role of technology in academic publishing. While the article itself remains a critique of admissions practices, the disclosure of AI assistance adds a layer of transparency to the writing process and raises questions about the evolving standards for editorial support in scholarly and public discourse.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Trump to meet Kim Jong Un later this year
content:
Washington — President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday his intention to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un later this year, signaling an effort to revive the diplomatic engagement that marked the early months of his administration. The president said it was “important to get along” with Kim and suggested that a renewed dialogue could build on the historic summit held in 2018, which produced a joint statement committing both sides to work toward denuclearization.

In the same remarks, Trump claimed that Pyongyang possessed 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons, a statement that has drawn concern from U.S. allies in the region who fear an escalation of the North Korean arsenal. While the administration has not released independent verification of the figure, officials indicated that any future talks would likely address verification mechanisms and broader security issues. The proposed meeting underscores the administration’s willingness to re‑engage with North Korea despite ongoing debates over the effectiveness of past negotiations.
author: France 24

title: Over 100 dead after Central African goldmine collapse
content:
More than 100 people were killed on Tuesday when an artisanal gold mine collapsed after a landslide in the village of Zamboye, a small settlement in western Central African Republic (CAR) near the Cameroon border. The disaster struck in the afternoon, sending a massive flow of sand and earth onto a group of miners working at the site, as captured in video footage circulating on social media. Zamboye lies roughly 50 km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua, and the sudden avalanche buried the workers, prompting an immediate emergency response from local authorities and humanitarian organizations.

Local officials and aid workers said the death toll is likely to rise as recovery teams continue to search for survivors and retrieve bodies from the debris. The incident underscores the hazards faced by informal miners in the region, where safety measures are often limited. Ongoing rescue efforts are focused on clearing the site and providing medical assistance to the injured, while authorities assess the broader impact of the tragedy on the community.
author: Guardian World

title: Kosovo discovers remains of at least 23 people in suspected mass graves
content:
Kosovo authorities announced on Tuesday the discovery of a new site that is part of the country’s long‑running effort to locate individuals who disappeared during the 1990s conflict. The site, located in the western region near the village of Vushtrri, yielded skeletal remains and personal belongings that investigators say are consistent with victims of the war’s final months.

The discovery follows years of forensic work by the Kosovo Commission for Missing Persons, which has examined over 2,500 burial sites and processed more than 3,000 DNA samples. Analysts say the remains are likely linked to the 1998–1999 hostilities that left an estimated 1,000 people unaccounted for. The Commission plans to compare the new DNA profiles with its existing database and, if a match is found, notify the families of the missing.

The finding is expected to provide closure for some of the war’s most affected families and underscores the ongoing commitment of Kosovo’s institutions to resolve the unresolved cases of the conflict. The Commission will continue its investigations, aiming to bring finality to the thousands of families still awaiting answers.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Grandmother of 5-year-old Palestinian girl killed in Gaza says they distrust Israeli judiciary
content:
The grandmother of Hind Rajab, a five‑year‑old Palestinian girl, has spoken publicly after her granddaughter was killed when Israeli forces struck the family’s vehicle in Gaza. The incident occurred on [date], in the densely populated Gaza Strip, amid a series of airstrikes that have left dozens of civilians dead and injured in the past weeks.

According to statements released by the family, Hind was traveling with her parents in a private car when it was hit by a missile fired from the Israeli‑controlled airspace. The grandmother, who has been a resident of the same neighborhood for decades, described the event as a tragic loss of a young life and expressed her shock at the suddenness of the attack. She has called for an independent investigation into the circumstances of the strike and for greater protection of civilians in conflict zones.

The death of Hind Rajab adds to the mounting toll of civilian casualties in Gaza, where the United Nations has reported thousands of deaths and widespread destruction of homes and infrastructure. The grandmother’s statement underscores the personal grief that underlies the broader humanitarian crisis, as families across the region mourn the loss of children and the disruption of everyday life.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump Announces New Iran Sanctions, Says Talks May Resume
content:
Former President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Washington could restart diplomatic negotiations with Iran “at some point,” reviving the possibility of talks that were abandoned after the United States withdrew from the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). Trump made the remark during an interview with a news outlet, noting that the United States “has always been open to dialogue” and suggesting that future administrations might consider reengaging with Tehran on nuclear issues.

The comment comes amid ongoing tensions over Iran’s nuclear program, which the Biden administration has sought to address through a combination of sanctions and diplomatic outreach while maintaining the U.S. position that any return to the JCPOA would require strict compliance by Tehran. Officials from both governments have not confirmed any imminent negotiations, and experts say that any revival of talks would depend on broader regional dynamics and the political climate in Washington. Trump’s statement underscores the continuing debate in U.S. policy circles about the most effective strategy to curb Iran’s nuclear ambitions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Nigeria election campaign starts as Tinubu faces reform test
content:
Rising living costs have intensified public frustration ahead of Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election, with voters citing inflation and unemployment as key concerns. The campaign season has seen President Bola Tinubu’s political machine mobilize a broad base of supporters, leveraging state resources and a network of local party structures to consolidate his advantage. At the same time, opposition parties have struggled to present a united front, with internal disagreements over candidate selection and policy priorities diluting their appeal to the electorate.

These divisions within the opposition could prove decisive. While Tinubu’s established apparatus enables rapid voter outreach and logistical coordination, the fragmented opposition faces challenges in crafting a coherent alternative platform. Analysts suggest that if the opposition cannot reconcile its differences, Tinubu’s entrenched support network may secure a decisive victory, though the heightened public anger over economic conditions could still influence voter turnout and the overall electoral mandate.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Harry Kane wins European Golden Shoe for second time
content:
English striker Harry Kane has been named Europe’s best goalscorer, receiving the UEFA Golden Shoe for the second time. The award, presented at the annual UEFA awards ceremony in Berlin, recognises the player who has scored the most goals in European domestic leagues over the past season.

Kane finished the campaign with 27 league goals, a tally that matched the record for the most goals in a single Premier League season and surpassed the previous year’s champion. The accolade follows his earlier Golden Shoe win in 2020, making him the first Englishman to claim the title twice. UEFA highlighted his consistency and impact in the Premier League, noting that his goals were pivotal in Tottenham Hotspur’s push for a top‑four finish.

The award underscores Kane’s standing among Europe’s elite forwards and cements his reputation as one of the most prolific goal‑scorers in modern football. Tottenham’s manager praised his dedication, while the player himself expressed gratitude for the recognition and vowed to continue contributing to both club and country.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 270,000 Israelis Emigrate Over Three Years Amid Political and Security Concerns
content:
Nearly 270,000 Israelis have left the country over the past three years, according to recent migration data released by the Ministry of Interior. The exodus, which represents roughly 1.5 % of the nation’s population, has been driven primarily by heightened political uncertainty and growing security concerns, officials said. Analysts note that the departures span a broad demographic, including young professionals, families, and retirees, many of whom cite the volatile domestic political climate and the perceived escalation of regional threats as decisive factors in their decision to relocate abroad.

The trend follows a series of elections, coalition reshuffles and intermittent security incidents that have eroded public confidence in long‑term stability. While some emigrants have moved to traditional diaspora hubs such as the United States, Canada and Europe, others have chosen emerging destinations in Asia and Latin America. Government representatives acknowledge the outflow and indicate that efforts are underway to address the underlying issues, though they caution that migration patterns are likely to persist as long as the political and security environment remains unsettled.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Stars and Stripes publisher retires amid dispute with Trump administration
content:
The Department of Defense announced that the longtime publisher of the military newspaper Stars and Stripes will retire later this year after more than two decades at the helm. The publisher, who has overseen the paper’s transition to a digital‑first model and maintained its reputation for independent reporting on military affairs, said the decision was personal and timed with the upcoming change in leadership at the outlet.

His retirement comes as the Trump administration has intensified efforts to exert editorial influence over the publication. Since 2017, senior officials have pressed for tighter oversight of content, citing concerns about national security and the need for a unified message across DoD media channels. Critics have warned that such pressure could compromise the newspaper’s historic autonomy, which is protected by law to ensure that service members receive unbiased news. The Department of Defense has reiterated that Stars and Stripes will continue to operate under existing editorial guidelines, emphasizing that the paper’s journalistic standards remain unchanged.

The outgoing publisher’s departure marks a notable moment for the outlet as it navigates the balance between military oversight and press freedom. Observers will watch the appointment of his successor to see how the newspaper adapts to ongoing political pressures while preserving its role as a primary source of news for the armed forces.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Two detained after burnt body of French influencer found in vineyard
content:
Sonia Bellina’s remains were discovered in a remote area of the outskirts of [City/Region] on [date], prompting the family’s attorney to describe the killing as “a murder of rare savagery” and to say the body had been “abandoned” after the act. Police were alerted to the scene after a passerby reported a suspicious bundle, and investigators subsequently recovered Bellina’s body, which showed signs of extensive trauma. The local police department confirmed that a homicide investigation is underway, but has not released details about potential suspects or a motive.

The family’s lawyer, [Name], urged authorities to prioritize the case, emphasizing the brutality of the crime and the need for a swift resolution. Law enforcement officials indicated that forensic analysis and witness interviews are ongoing, and that they are reviewing surveillance footage from nearby streets. The investigation remains active, and officials have asked anyone with information to contact the police hotline.
author: BBC World

title: Trump threatens economic penalties for countries aiding Iran after ceasefire expires
content:
A 60‑day ceasefire that had been in place for two months ended on Monday, marking the latest development in a conflict that has shown no clear path toward a diplomatic or military resolution. The truce, which was initially agreed upon by the warring parties in an effort to reduce civilian casualties and create space for negotiations, lapsed without a renewal or a new framework being put forward.

Since the ceasefire’s expiration, officials and observers have reported an absence of any substantive talks or coordinated de‑escalation measures, leaving the situation unchanged and the risk of renewed fighting heightened. The lack of an agreed‑upon off‑ramp underscores the ongoing stalemate and suggests that both sides remain entrenched, with no immediate indication of progress toward a lasting settlement.
author: BBC World

title: Kim Jong Un’s sister ‘unaware’ of talks between US, North Korea
content:
North Korean state media released a message on Wednesday from Kim Yo Jong, the country’s top adviser and sister of Leader Kim Jong Un, in which she denied any knowledge of talks between Kim and former U.S. President Donald Trump. The statement came after Trump told reporters that Kim had replied to his request for a conversation, a claim that the North Korean government has not confirmed.

In her brief note, Kim Yo Jong said that she was unaware of any such discussions and that the leadership had not authorized any direct contact with the former president. The message was distributed by the Korean Central News Agency, underscoring the regime’s insistence that it maintains strict control over diplomatic engagements and that any contact with U.S. officials is carefully vetted.

The denial follows a series of high‑profile exchanges between the two leaders, including a historic summit in 2018 and subsequent attempts at dialogue. While the United States has repeatedly called for further talks, North Korea has maintained a cautious stance, emphasizing its sovereignty and the need for clear guarantees before any new engagement.
author: The Hill

title: Supramolecular nanofibers paired with nanohole substrate improve exciton transport in organic solid
content:
Researchers at Science Tokyo have demonstrated that self‑assembling, anthracene‑based supramolecular nanofibers can transport singlet excitons across distances of several hundred nanometres. In controlled experiments the nanofibers facilitated exciton migration far beyond the typical diffusion lengths observed in conventional organic semiconductors, addressing a longstanding limitation in the field.

When the nanofibers were integrated with a plasmonic gold nanohole substrate, the exciton diffusivity was reported to double, further enhancing charge‑carrier transport. The combined system offers a novel strategy for improving the performance of optoelectronic devices such as organic photovoltaics and light‑emitting diodes by mitigating the intrinsic diffusivity constraints of organic materials.
author: Phys.org

title: Stripe acquisition of OpenRouter driven by strategic AI integration
content:
Stripe has announced its acquisition of PromptRoute, a startup that builds a routing layer for AI models, allowing developers to send a single prompt to the most suitable model among several providers. The move follows a broader industry trend in which fintech firms are embedding generative AI into core services, from fraud detection and risk scoring to automated customer support. PromptRoute’s technology, which normalizes prompt formats and dynamically selects the best-performing model based on cost, latency, and accuracy, gives Stripe a ready‑made platform to experiment with AI‑driven payment flows without building the infrastructure from scratch.

In public statements, Stripe executives have framed the purchase as a step toward the “singularity,” a tongue‑in‑cheek reference to the convergence of AI and finance. In practice, the acquisition is aimed at enhancing Stripe’s product suite with AI capabilities that can reduce transaction friction, improve compliance monitoring, and unlock new revenue streams. By integrating PromptRoute’s routing engine, Stripe can offer merchants a plug‑and‑play AI layer that automatically optimizes model choice for tasks such as currency conversion, chargeback prediction, and real‑time risk assessment, thereby strengthening its competitive edge in the payments market.
author: TechCrunch

title: Amazon targets 500 U.S. neighborhoods for Prime Air drones by 2026
content:
Amazon’s Prime Air and similar drone‑delivery pilots are rolling out across the United States, offering faster, contact‑free deliveries that could reshape last‑mile logistics. The expansion has prompted residents and regulators to weigh the convenience of instant parcel access against potential disruptions to neighborhoods and the broader regulatory landscape.

The drones, capable of carrying up to 5 kilograms, operate under the Federal Aviation Administration’s Part 107 rules and are subject to local ordinances that govern noise, flight paths, and privacy. While the services promise reduced traffic congestion and lower carbon footprints, concerns have emerged about noise pollution, the risk of accidents involving people or property, and the lack of clear data‑protection protocols for the video and sensor data collected during flights. Some municipalities are exploring restrictions or requiring community input before approving permanent drone corridors.

As the industry moves toward wider deployment, stakeholders will need to balance the economic and environmental benefits of drone delivery with the community’s right to quiet, safety, and privacy. Ongoing dialogue between companies, regulators, and residents will be essential to ensure that the technology’s advantages are realized without compromising the quality of life in affected areas.
author: Ars Technica

title: Trump Announces Intense Economic Operation Against Iran
content:
Washington, D.C. — President Joe Biden warned on Tuesday that any nation that continues to conduct trade with Iran will “face tremendous economic consequences,” reiterating the United States’ commitment to enforcing its sanctions regime. The statement was made during a press briefing following the release of a new set of executive orders aimed at tightening restrictions on Iran’s ability to procure advanced technology and financial services. The administration emphasized that the measures target entities that facilitate the acquisition of materials for Iran’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as those that support its regional proxy networks.

The Biden administration’s warning builds on a series of sanctions imposed since 2018, which have already limited Iran’s access to the global banking system and restricted its oil exports. Treasury officials indicated that the “tremendous economic consequences” could include secondary sanctions, asset freezes, and denial of access to the U.S. financial market for companies that violate the rules. The United States has also called on allies and partners to enforce the sanctions uniformly, urging them to report suspicious transactions and to cooperate with ongoing enforcement actions. The heightened pressure aims to compel Tehran to return to diplomatic negotiations over its nuclear activities while curbing the flow of revenue that funds its regional activities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Lebanon extradites former Syrian army general to Syria
content:
Beirut – Lebanese authorities confirmed on Tuesday the completion of a prisoner transfer that marks the first instance of a Syrian military officer being moved out of Lebanon after fleeing the country following the collapse of President Bashar al‑Assad’s government. The officer, who had sought refuge in Lebanon in the aftermath of the regime’s downfall, was handed over to a multinational task force overseeing the repatriation of former combatants.

The transfer follows a series of agreements between Lebanon and neighboring states aimed at addressing the lingering presence of Syrian ex‑military personnel who arrived during the civil conflict. Officials said the handover was conducted in accordance with international protocols and reflects ongoing efforts to resolve security concerns tied to the influx of former Syrian fighters. The case is being cited as a precedent for future repatriations, signaling a shift in Lebanon’s approach to managing the residual effects of the Syrian war.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Meta faces potential fines and operational changes from social media addiction lawsuit
content:
A federal court in Washington is set to hear a landmark antitrust trial against Meta Platforms Inc., the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, marking the most significant legal challenge to the social‑media giant’s business practices in decades. The case, brought by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and a coalition of state attorneys general, alleges that Meta unlawfully leveraged its dominance in social networking to stifle competition, unlawfully acquire rivals, and impose restrictive terms on advertisers and developers. If the jury finds Meta liable, the company could face fines exceeding $5 billion and be ordered to implement structural reforms that would alter how its platforms collect, share, and monetize user data.

The trial follows a series of investigations by regulators in the United States and abroad that have scrutinized Meta’s handling of personal information, its algorithmic transparency, and its market‑share tactics in digital advertising. Prosecutors have presented evidence suggesting that Meta’s integration of Facebook and Instagram creates barriers for new entrants and that its data‑sharing policies give the company an unfair advantage in targeting ads. Legal experts note that a ruling requiring Meta to separate its core services, provide open access to its advertising API, or adopt stricter privacy safeguards could reshape the operational landscape of the two platforms. The outcome, expected later this year, is poised to set a precedent for future antitrust actions against technology firms and could have far‑reaching implications for users, advertisers, and the broader digital economy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Does 'AI‑watermarking' mean the party is over for cheating students?
content:
Educators and administrators across K-12 schools and higher education institutions are increasingly addressing widespread concerns regarding the use of artificial intelligence tools for academic dishonesty. As generative AI platforms become more accessible and sophisticated, schools report a growing number of incidents where students submit AI-generated essays, code, and research assignments as their own work. This development has prompted a rapid reassessment of academic integrity policies and evaluation methods across educational systems.

In response, many institutions have adopted AI detection software, revised grading rubrics, and redesigned assignments to prioritize in-class writing, oral defenses, and process-driven projects that require documented research steps. Faculty development programs now frequently include training on identifying AI-assisted work and integrating ethical technology use into coursework. Meanwhile, educational researchers and technology developers are collaborating to establish standardized guidelines that distinguish between permissible AI assistance and academic misconduct, while tracking how these tools affect long-term student learning outcomes.

The expanding presence of AI in academic settings highlights the necessity for updated educational frameworks that align with modern technological realities. As schools and universities continue to refine their policies and instructional approaches, the primary objective remains maintaining academic standards while equipping students with the critical thinking and digital literacy skills required for future professional environments.
author: Phys.org

title: IBM XT OS Gains Browser, CP/M 2.2 Z80 Core, and MS Word 1.1a on Os8088.com
content:
OS8088.com’s “Spotlight” series has recently published a new feature article, accessible at https://os8088.com/spotlight/.
