author: Medical Xpress

title: Bronze Age brands identified in Arabian desert oasis pottery
content:
Archaeologists have confirmed that branding practices pre‑date modern capitalist societies.  An international research team headed by Marta Luciani of the University of Vienna reports that Bronze Age traders in northwestern Arabia used distinctive marks on pottery to identify producers, a form of early brand that dates back roughly 3,200 years.

The study, based on excavations at the oasis of Qurayyah, uncovered two‑colour painted vessels bearing consistent, stylised symbols.  The marks, found on a wide range of ceramic wares, indicate a standardized production system and suggest that goods were tracked and possibly traded across regional networks.  The discovery provides the first concrete evidence of commercial branding in a non‑capitalist economy of the ancient Near East.

These findings broaden the historical understanding of early market mechanisms and demonstrate that the concept of a brand—an identifiable mark linked to a specific producer—has deep roots in human trade practices.  The research underscores the sophistication of Bronze Age commerce in Arabia and invites further investigation into the spread of branding across ancient societies.
author: Phys.org

title: Brazil Bus Crash Kills 23, Injures 5 in Parana
content:
A bus en route to hospitals near Curitiba was involved in an accident on a local road, according to preliminary reports. The vehicle was traveling northward from the city toward a cluster of medical facilities when the incident occurred. No details about the exact location or the time of day have been released by local authorities.

Investigators are examining the circumstances of the crash, but the cause remains unknown. No official statement has yet confirmed whether there were injuries or fatalities, and authorities have not released a casualty count. The incident has prompted a temporary suspension of
author: Al Jazeera

title: Kennedy Center Board Rejects Immediate Restoration of Trump Name
content:
A local entertainment venue has become the focus of a legal dispute after a court ordered the removal of a former president’s name from its signage. The ruling, issued last month by a regional court, cited violations of a trademark agreement and demanded that the venue cease using the name in all promotional materials and on the building itself. Opponents of the venue’s continued use of the name argue that the establishment appears “intent on defying” the court order, suggesting a disregard for the judicial decision.

The venue’s management has responded that the name is integral to its brand identity and that they are reviewing the court’s directive. Legal analysts note that non‑compliance could result in fines or an injunction compelling the removal of the signage. The case remains pending, with a hearing scheduled for next week to determine whether the venue will comply with the order or face further sanctions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Canada pledges $50 million aid to Lebanon, condemns Israeli invasion
content:
Ottawa’s foreign affairs minister publicly denounced Israel’s recent military incursion into southern Lebanon, describing it as an “invasion” that violates Lebanese sovereignty. In a statement released on Tuesday, the minister urged all parties to respect international law and called for an immediate de‑escalation of hostilities that have displaced thousands of civilians and strained already fragile infrastructure in the crisis‑hit nation.

The Canadian government announced a new assistance package worth CAD 30 million, earmarked for emergency shelter, medical supplies, and food distribution to communities affected by the fighting. The aid, to be delivered through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency and local NGOs, aims to bolster Lebanon’s capacity to respond to the surge in displaced persons and to support reconstruction of damaged health facilities. Ottawa said the pledge underscores Canada’s commitment to Lebanon’s territorial integrity and to broader regional stability, while urging the international community to pursue diplomatic solutions to the conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Canada and US near completion of trade deal as deadline approaches
content:
Prime Minister Carney said the latest round of trade negotiations has achieved “significant progress,” as the two nations work to finalize remaining issues before a newly set weekend deadline for tariff adjustments. The statement was made during a press briefing on Thursday, where Carney emphasized that both sides are focused on resolving outstanding points that have delayed the implementation of the agreed‑upon tariff schedule.

Negotiators are now concentrating on the final details of market access, rules of origin and dispute‑resolution mechanisms, with the goal of meeting the deadline that will determine whether the provisional tariff reductions take effect. Officials from both governments have indicated that, if the deadline is met, the revised tariff framework could boost bilateral trade flows and provide greater certainty for businesses operating across the border.
author: BBC World

title: Human remains found at Lake Mead as water levels fall
content:
Human remains were found in Lake Mead on August 16, according to a report by USA Today, marking the latest grim discovery in the reservoir that supplies water to the Las Vegas area. The National Park Service said the body showed no signs of suspicious activity, and investigators are treating it as a routine search for missing persons.

Lake Mead has been experiencing record low water levels for several years, raising concerns about water supply and environmental conditions. The discovery follows a series of similar findings in recent months, prompting authorities to review safety protocols and increase monitoring of the lake’s shoreline. While the circumstances of this particular case remain unclear, the NPS has confirmed that the investigation is ongoing.

The incident underscores the challenges facing the region as water scarcity and climate change continue to affect the reservoir’s capacity. Officials have urged anyone with information to come forward, and the search for the individual remains a priority for local law‑enforcement and park officials.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Trump nominates White House health adviser Heidi Overton as FDA commissioner
content:
President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social on Wednesday that he has nominated Dr. Heidi Overton to serve as the next Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. Overton, a physician with extensive experience in public health, currently serves as a senior domestic policy adviser on health matters in the White House. Her appointment follows a period of significant turnover at the FDA, during which several senior officials have resigned or been reassigned.

The agency has been described as “roiled” by the exodus of top staff, raising concerns about its capacity to oversee drug approvals, medical device regulation, and food safety standards. Overton’s background in clinical medicine and her role in shaping national health policy are seen as assets that could help restore stability and continuity within the FDA’s leadership. If confirmed by the Senate, she would assume responsibility for steering the agency’s regulatory agenda amid ongoing scrutiny over its decision‑making processes and workforce challenges.

The nomination is expected to prompt a Senate confirmation hearing, where Overton’s qualifications and policy positions will be examined. Her leadership will be closely watched by industry stakeholders, consumer advocacy groups, and health professionals as the FDA continues to navigate complex regulatory and public health issues.
author: The Hill

title: Book chronicles rise of desert toad psychedelic and its promoter
content:
Kimon de Greef’s new book, *The Ego Trip*, traces the history of a powerful psychedelic compound that originates from the secretions of certain toads. The narrative follows the drug’s journey from its natural source to its emergence as a sought‑after psychoactive substance, detailing the scientific and cultural forces that have shaped its reputation.

The work centers on a controversial figure who claimed that the compound possesses extraordinary abilities, and it examines the claims through interviews, laboratory reports, and historical documents. Olivia Goldhill, a researcher and journalist, uncovered the story through a combination of archival research and firsthand accounts, revealing how the drug’s allure has evolved over decades and how it has been embraced by both the scientific community and countercultural movements.

*The Ego Trip* offers a comprehensive look at the intersection of biology, mysticism, and modern drug culture, providing readers with a nuanced understanding of how a simple toad secretion has become a symbol of altered consciousness. The book has been praised for its thorough research and balanced presentation, and it is expected to contribute significantly to discussions about psychedelic substances and their place in contemporary society.
author: New Scientist

title: Trump expected to pick conservative policy wonk Heidi Overton to lead FDA
content:
A state legislator has drawn attention this week for her outspoken positions on several health‑related issues. In recent interviews and public statements, she reaffirmed her opposition to abortion, expressed caution about the use of peptide‑based therapies, and advocated for stricter limits on vaccine mandates. The lawmaker’s platform, which emphasizes personal choice and limited governmental intervention in medical decisions, has become a focal point of debate among constituents and health officials.

Critics from the Medical Association of Health Administrators (MAHA) have publicly challenged her stance, arguing that the proposed restrictions could undermine public health initiatives and impede the adoption of emerging treatments. MAHA officials have highlighted data supporting the safety and efficacy of both peptide therapies and vaccination programs, contending that the legislator’s positions may conflict with established medical guidelines. Supporters, however, maintain that her approach reflects community concerns about over‑medicalization and the preservation of individual autonomy.

The controversy underscores an ongoing clash between policy makers and health professionals over the balance between regulatory oversight and personal freedom in medical care. As the legislative session progresses, the lawmaker’s proposals are expected to face further scrutiny in committee hearings, where both her supporters and opponents will present evidence to shape the final outcome.
author: Ars Technica

title: Trump Claims North Korea Has 57 Powerful Nuclear Weapons
content:
Former President Donald Trump has reiterated concerns about the United States’ military posture on the Korean Peninsula, following his recent announcement that U.S. forces would reduce the frequency of joint drills with South Korea. In a statement issued earlier this week, Trump said the decision to scale back exercises was intended to avoid sending an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. The move comes amid heightened tensions in the region, with the U.S. and South Korean militaries traditionally conducting large‑scale, regular drills as a deterrent against North Korean provocations.

The reduction in joint exercises, announced by the U.S. Department of Defense, will see a shift from biannual to quarterly training sessions, according to the Pentagon. Trump’s remarks, made on a campaign platform, echo his longstanding criticism of what he views as overly aggressive U.S. military engagement in East Asia. Analysts note that the change could affect the U.S. alliance with Seoul, though officials have emphasized that core deterrence capabilities remain intact.

While the U.S. and South Korean governments have confirmed that the core components of their defense partnership will continue, the decision has sparked debate among policymakers and military experts. Some argue that the scaled‑back drills may reduce deterrence, while others contend that a more measured approach could lower the risk of accidental escalation. The U.S. will likely monitor North Korea’s response closely as it adjusts its own posture in the coming months.
author: Euronews

title: Imran Khan moved to hospital, prompting talk of political negotiations
content:
Former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was transferred from his prison cell to a hospital in Islamabad on Monday for medical treatment, according to the Interior Ministry. The move follows a series of health‑related complaints that had prompted a medical review of the former leader’s condition. Khan, who has been in custody since his arrest in August, is being treated for a chronic illness that has reportedly worsened in recent weeks.

The transfer has sparked speculation among political analysts that the government may be open to new negotiations with Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek‑e‑Insaf party. In a statement, the ministry said the decision was made solely on medical grounds and that no political concessions were involved. Nonetheless, opposition leaders and PTI officials have called for a dialogue to address the broader legal and political disputes surrounding Khan’s case.

Observers note that the move could signal a shift in the government’s approach to the high‑profile case, potentially paving the way for a broader settlement. However, no official policy changes have been announced, and the Interior Ministry reiterated that the transfer is temporary and focused on Khan’s health. The situation remains closely monitored by domestic and international stakeholders.
author: DW World

title: US and Canada finalize tariff‑free trade agreement
content:
Washington — President Donald Trump announced a new trade agreement with Canada that eliminates tariffs on agricultural products and a broad range of U.S. manufactured goods exported to the neighboring country. The pact, finalized after weeks of negotiations between the United States Trade Representative’s office and Canadian officials, removes the 10‑percent duty previously applied to dairy, poultry, and certain grain shipments, and lifts the 5‑percent levy on automotive parts, machinery, and technology components. Under the terms of the deal, U.S. exporters will receive immediate market access, while Canadian authorities have pledged to streamline customs procedures to accelerate the flow of goods across the border.

The tariff‑free arrangement is expected to boost U.S. farm income and support manufacturing sectors that rely on cross‑border supply chains, according to data from the Department of Agriculture and the Commerce Department. Analysts note that the agreement aligns with the broader objective of strengthening North American trade ties and may serve as a template for future negotiations with other partners. The administration indicated that the deal will be implemented within 30 days, pending standard regulatory reviews, and will be monitored for compliance through quarterly reporting mechanisms.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Labour urges Reform UK deputy leader to apologise to firefighters over heat remark
content:
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, has urged Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice to apologise for his recent remarks encouraging the public to “enjoy” the summer’s extreme heat. The comments came after a series of severe wildfires that have forced widespread evacuations and destroyed homes across the country. Phillipson said the party’s stance on Reform’s net‑zero agenda has already alienated many voters, and that Tice’s tone was “inappropriate and insensitive” to those who have fought the fires.

Tice’s remarks, made this week on social media, were widely criticised by emergency services officials and community groups. Firefighters who have battled the blazes cited the lack of public support and the need for urgent action to address climate‑related risks. Labour’s call for an apology follows a broader debate over Reform’s environmental policies, with critics arguing that the party’s approach to net zero is too aggressive and politically damaging.

The Labour Party’s appeal for an apology underscores the growing pressure on Reform to address the public’s concerns about climate change and emergency preparedness. If Tice does not respond, Phillipson has indicated that the party will continue to highlight the disconnect between Reform’s rhetoric and the lived experiences of those affected by the recent wildfires.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Google Pixel Watch 5 adds new health software but lacks full feature rollout
content:
The Google Pixel Watch 5 has proven to be the most challenging model in the Pixel Watch line to evaluate. While the device’s hardware remains largely unchanged—identical dimensions, the same Snapdragon Wear 4100+ processor, and only a marginal battery improvement—the watch’s new pyrite‑satin case finish marks the most visible cosmetic upgrade.

The primary focus of this year’s release lies in software, with Google expanding the Health app’s capabilities and integrating an AI coach that debuted with the Fitbit Air earlier in the year. The updated watch promises new health metrics, including blood‑pressure monitoring, insulin‑resistance trend analysis, and nightly sleep‑breathing metrics. However, reviewers have noted that these features are not yet available on the device.

Despite the lack of the promised health tools, the Pixel Watch 5’s continued emphasis on software enhancements underscores Google’s strategy to differentiate its wearable through data and AI rather than hardware changes. The Verge’s full review details the watch’s performance and the current status of its health features.
author: The Verge

title: No, Italy’s Lake Como didn’t dry up
content:
A viral TikTok video claiming that Lake Como in northern Italy has vanished following a "geological rupture" has been confirmed false by fact-checkers and geological experts. The sensational post, which spread rapidly across social media, featured dramatic footage and photographs purporting to show the iconic lake completely dry. Authorities and scientific observers have stated unequivocally that no such event has occurred and that the lake remains intact.

Analysis of the viral content reveals that all accompanying images and video clips were artificially generated using AI tools rather than documenting real conditions. While Lake Como has experienced lower water levels in recent months, this reduction is the result of prolonged drought affecting the region, not seismic or tectonic activity. High-resolution satellite imagery consistently shows the lake retaining substantial volume, with shoreline changes aligning with documented climate-related water fluctuations.

Environmental agencies continue to track regional water levels as part of routine drought monitoring efforts. The episode highlights the increasing circulation of AI-generated misinformation and reinforces the importance of cross-referencing viral claims with verified data. Lake Como remains a fully existing body of water, and no geological catastrophe has taken place.
author: France 24

title: US Regime Change: 70 Years of Interventions and Their Impact
content:
U.S. foreign policy has repeatedly involved covert and overt interventions aimed at altering the political leadership of other nations, a pattern that has produced significant human and financial costs.  The most cited example is the 1953 CIA‑backed coup in Iran that overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh and installed Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, a move that destabilized the region for decades.  Since then, the United States has pursued regime‑change objectives in Iraq (2003), Libya (2011), Syria (2015), and Afghanistan (2001), each operation accompanied by substantial civilian casualties, displacement, and long‑term security challenges.

These interventions have consistently involved large budgets—ranging from the $2 billion spent on the 1953 operation to the $2.4 trillion projected cost of the Iraq war—and have generated ongoing humanitarian crises.  In Iraq alone, more than 200,000 civilians have died, and the country remains fragmented by sectarian conflict.  Similar patterns appear in Syria, where the civil war has displaced millions and left the infrastructure in ruins, and in Libya, where the power vacuum has fueled extremist groups and regional instability.

The recurring theme across these cases is that U.S. attempts to engineer regime changes often lead to unintended consequences, including prolonged conflict, regional destabilization, and immense human suffering.  As the United States continues to engage in foreign interventions, the historical record underscores the need for a careful assessment of both the strategic objectives and the profound costs associated with altering sovereign governments.
author: Al Jazeera

title: India beats Pakistan 5-3 to finish second in Hockey World Cup 2026 pool
content:
India defeated Pakistan 5‑3 in their Pool D encounter, securing the runner‑up spot with six points after the group’s final round of matches. The win kept India unbeaten in the pool stage and ensured they finish ahead of Pakistan, who remain third with three points. England, meanwhile, topped the same pool by winning all three of their games, accumulating nine points and confirming their place at the summit of Pool D.

The standings set the stage for the upcoming knockout phase, with England and India advancing as the pool’s leading teams. Pakistan’s loss leaves them out of contention for the quarter‑finals, while the remaining teams in the tournament will now focus on their next fixtures based on the final pool rankings.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Stanford study finds lower heat tolerance limits and higher risk for elderly
content:
Stanford University researchers have published new findings indicating that the human body’s tolerance to heat is lower than previously believed, with age emerging as a significant risk factor. The study, conducted by the university’s School of Medicine, analyzed physiological responses to elevated temperatures in a diverse cohort of participants ranging from young adults to seniors. Results show that heat stress thresholds drop markedly as people age, suggesting that older adults may reach dangerous levels of core temperature at lower environmental heat loads.

The investigation measured core body temperature, heart rate, and sweat production while subjects were exposed to controlled heat environments. Researchers found that individuals over 65 reached critical core temperatures at ambient temperatures 3 to 5 degrees Celsius lower than the limits established in earlier research. The study also highlighted that older adults exhibit reduced sweat gland function and impaired cardiovascular responses, which together compromise the body’s ability to dissipate heat. These physiological changes underscore the heightened vulnerability of the elderly population to heat‑related illnesses, especially during heatwaves.

The findings carry implications for public health guidelines and emergency response planning, particularly in the context of rising global temperatures. By redefining safe exposure limits and emphasizing age‑specific risk, the research advocates for targeted heat‑wave advisories and preventive measures for older adults. The Stanford team recommends further studies to refine heat tolerance metrics and to develop interventions that mitigate heat‑related morbidity among aging populations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israel opens tenders for West Bank settlement project
content:
Jerusalem – Israeli officials have confirmed plans to develop new housing and infrastructure in the E1 zone, an area east of the city that would link existing settlements to Jerusalem and effectively bisect the occupied West Bank. The proposal, which would create a continuous Israeli presence across the territory, has been met with condemnation from a broad coalition of international actors who argue that it undermines the viability of a two‑state solution.

The United Nations, the European Union and several individual governments have reiterated that the construction would violate international law and exacerbate tensions in the region. Palestinian leaders have warned that the move could trigger widespread unrest, while Israeli authorities contend the development is necessary for security and demographic considerations. Diplomatic discussions continue as the international community seeks to balance settlement activity with efforts to revive negotiations toward a negotiated settlement.
author: BBC World

title: US and South Korea halve Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise after Trump order
content:
The Pentagon and the Republic of Korea’s armed forces confirmed on Wednesday that the two‑nation Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise will be shortened in response to a directive from President Donald Trump. The drill, which began on Monday, is a large‑scale joint training operation that typically runs for a full week.

Under the new schedule, the exercise will now conclude on August 21, six days earlier than the originally planned August 27 finish date. A Defense Department statement said the decision to cut the duration was made to reduce the overall scope of the exercise, in line with the President’s request.

Both sides will adjust their plans accordingly, with the shortened timeline expected to affect the number of maneuvers and the duration of combat simulations conducted during the drill.
author: The Hill

title: Researchers investigate how cat urine scent marks retain identity information over time
content:
**Scent marks remain reliable signals long after the scent is released**  
Researchers have long noted that many mammals, birds, and reptiles use urine and other scent marks to communicate across space and time. These marks persist in the environment even after the animal has left, allowing individuals to assess territory boundaries, reproductive status, and social hierarchy. However, the volatile odor molecules that compose these marks are subject to evaporation, degradation, and chemical transformation, raising the question of how a scent can still convey accurate information about its source.

Recent studies have shown that scent marks are not simple, single‑molecule signals but complex mixtures of compounds with varying chemical stability. Certain hydrocarbons and fatty acids remain intact for days or weeks, while more volatile pheromones provide immediate, short‑term cues. Animals have evolved highly sensitive olfactory receptors tuned to detect these persistent components, enabling them to identify the individual who deposited the mark, its sex, reproductive condition, and even its recent health status. Laboratory experiments tracking the decay of specific urinary compounds confirm that the most informative molecules are those least affected by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and microbial activity.

These findings underscore the sophistication of chemical communication in the animal kingdom. By relying on a suite of stable and transient molecules, creatures can maintain reliable social and territorial information over extended periods, ensuring effective navigation of complex ecological landscapes.
author: Phys.org

title: Sachin Bansal’s fintech Navi raises first outside capital with $100M Prosus investment
content:
Navi, the fintech startup known for its digital banking platform, has announced a new investment as it moves toward an initial public offering.  While the terms of the deal—including the amount and the identity of the investor—have not been disclosed, the funding is intended to support the company’s expansion plans.

The capital injection comes at a critical juncture for Navi, which is preparing to list on a major stock exchange in the coming months.  The additional resources are expected to help the firm broaden its product suite, enhance its technology infrastructure, and strengthen its balance sheet ahead of the IPO, positioning it for a more robust market debut.

With the investment in place, Navi aims to solidify its competitive standing in the fintech space and provide a stronger foundation for long‑term growth.  The move is seen as a strategic step to ensure the company is well positioned for the heightened scrutiny and capital demands that accompany a public listing.
author: TechCrunch

title: Israel Numbers Palestinian Detainee Foreheads in Qabatiya Raid
content:
Palestinian news outlets reported that a man was found with the number “44” written on his forehead after a raid in the West Bank town of Qabatiya. The incident occurred during a security operation that had been carried out earlier in the day, according to local sources. The man was reportedly injured and was taken to a nearby medical facility for treatment.

The raid, which was conducted by Israeli forces, was part of a broader series of operations in the area aimed at detaining individuals suspected of involvement in recent unrest. While the exact reason for the number on the man’s forehead remains unclear, some observers suggest it could be an identification marker or a symbolic gesture related to the ongoing conflict. The local police have not yet released a statement regarding the man’s identity or the circumstances that led to the marking.

Authorities are investigating the incident, and no further details have been released at this time. The situation remains fluid, and observers are monitoring developments as additional information becomes available.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Jonathan Zimmerman critiques university hiring practices amid Jason Arday controversy
content:
Author Jonathan Zimmerman has recently highlighted the growing tension between merit-based evaluation and identity-focused criteria in higher education. In a piece published in a prominent academic journal, Zimmerman contends that the controversies surrounding former professor Jason Arday and a series of high-profile hiring decisions illustrate a broader shift in university policy away from evidence‑driven assessment toward ideological alignment.

Arday, a scholar in the humanities, was dismissed from his position after a lawsuit alleging discriminatory conduct. The case attracted widespread media coverage and prompted debates about the fairness of the university’s disciplinary procedures. Zimmerman argues that the swift removal of Arday, coupled with similar hiring controversies—such as appointments that emphasize a candidate’s identity background over scholarly credentials—demonstrate a pattern in which institutions prioritize ideological conformity over measurable academic performance. He cites data from recent tenure reviews and hiring panels that show an increasing weight given to diversity statements and political alignment.

Zimmerman’s analysis suggests that this trend may undermine the traditional standards of academic rigor and objectivity. By foregrounding identity politics in hiring and disciplinary processes, universities risk eroding the meritocratic foundations that have historically guided scholarly advancement. The argument underscores a need for clearer, evidence‑based criteria to maintain the integrity of academic evaluation.
author: The Hill

title: Offloading work tasks to AI comes with a cost—to our brains
content:
Government agencies and corporate policy teams are increasingly turning to generative artificial intelligence to accelerate the production of high-stakes policy documents amid compressed deadlines. In recent months, researchers and strategic advisors have reported that AI systems can generate comprehensive draft papers within minutes, delivering organized frameworks, structured arguments, and formatted citations that mirror traditional academic and institutional standards. This rapid output capability is prompting organizations to reassess their research workflows as they balance the demand for swift deliverables with the need for reliable analysis.

The underlying models synthesize information from vast training datasets to produce coherent policy narratives and reference lists
author: Phys.org

title: Study investigates leveraging quantum battery environmental sensitivity for better energy use
content:
Quantum batteries—devices that store energy through quantum mechanical effects—promise faster charging and higher efficiency than conventional batteries. Recent studies suggest that, in principle, these batteries could be charged more quickly by harnessing collective quantum phenomena, potentially transforming portable power and grid storage.

However, researchers have found that the act of connecting a quantum battery to a charger introduces quantum correlations between the two systems. These correlations can lock a portion of the stored energy within the combined battery‑charger complex, preventing it from being extracted as useful work. As a result, the amount of energy that can be delivered to a load is reduced, undermining some of the anticipated performance gains.

The findings highlight a critical challenge for practical quantum energy devices: while quantum effects can enhance storage and charging speeds, they also create entanglement that must be managed to avoid energy loss. Future research will need to develop strategies for decoupling or mitigating these correlations to fully realize the advantages of quantum batteries.
author: Phys.org

title: Australia mushroom killer's lawyers point to jury irregularities at appeal
content: Lawyers for Erin Patterson, the Australian woman convicted of a triple murder involving poisoned food, filed an application on Wednesday to overturn her conviction, alleging that the jury was not properly sequestered during the trial. The 51-year-old was found guilty last year of killing her husband's parents and an elderly aunt by serving them a beef Wellington lunch contaminated with lethal death cap mushrooms in 202
author: France 24

title: Palestinian Authority Lacks Budget for Essential Services
content:
Annette Young announced the arrival of Joost Hiltermann, the International Crisis Group’s Special Adviser for the Middle East and North Africa and a senior training officer. Hiltermann will focus on strengthening the Group’s work in the region, particularly on the Palestinian Authority (PA) and its institutions.

Hiltermann argues that the PA’s financial crisis is not a sudden emergency but a prolonged process of institutional and economic erosion. He notes that the Authority has already lost much of its ability to deliver essential services, pay public‑sector salaries in full, maintain infrastructure, and support education and health care. These deficits are compounded by settlement expansion, settler violence and Israeli restrictions, which together create a hostile environment for Palestinian governance and economic stability.

The combination of ongoing settlement activity, security restrictions and financial pressures poses a continuing threat to Palestinian institutions and economic life. Hiltermann’s assessment underscores the need for sustained international attention to the PA’s capacity challenges and the broader conditions that shape its future.
author: France 24

title: Ukraine MPs Approve New Defence Minister After Reshuffle
content:
Ukraine’s parliament approved a new defence minister on Wednesday, a month after a controversial reshuffle that saw the dismissal of the popular former minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The decision follows a public backlash that erupted when Fedorov was removed, with critics arguing that the move undermined civilian oversight of the armed forces amid the ongoing war with Russia.

The new appointment comes a day after Fedorov released a video statement in which he urged the government to resume elections that have been postponed due to the Russian invasion. His call for democratic renewal was met with mixed reactions, as some saw it as a necessary step toward restoring normalcy, while others feared it could destabilise an already fragile political environment. The parliament’s approval of the new minister is therefore seen as both a response to domestic pressure and a signal that Kyiv remains focused on maintaining a robust defence posture.

With the new defence minister taking office, Ukraine continues to navigate the dual challenge of sustaining its military campaigns against Russian forces and addressing internal demands for political reform. The appointment underscores the government’s attempt to balance strategic security needs with growing calls for democratic processes, a balancing act that will shape Ukraine’s political landscape in the coming months.
author: France 24

title: Turkey rejects Israel's claims after strike on Syrian air base
content:
Turkey on Wednesday rejected what it described as “untenable allegations” from Israel concerning Ankara’s military posture in Syria after Israeli jets struck the Abu al‑Duhur air base near Aleppo, close to the Turkish border. Israel said the strike was a response to intelligence indicating that Syria was about to allow Turkish forces to operate on its territory, a claim Turkey dismissed as baseless. The Israeli attack, which targeted the Syrian facility on Tuesday, prompted an official protest from the Turkish foreign ministry, which condemned the violation of Syrian sovereignty and warned against any escalation that could destabilise the region.

The United States also weighed in, with a senior envoy labeling the Israeli airstrike an “unnecessary escalation” and urging restraint from all parties. The incident adds to a series of cross‑border tensions involving Israel, Syria and Turkey, where each side has expressed concerns over security and the potential deployment of foreign troops. Observers note that the episode underscores the fragile security dynamics along the northern Syrian frontier, and diplomatic efforts are expected to focus on preventing further military confrontations.
author: France 24

title: Ukrainian anti-corruption probe targets Zelensky office after ex-defence minister urges elections
content:
Ukrainian anti‑corruption agencies announced on Wednesday that they have opened investigations into senior officials within President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office. The probe comes a day after the country’s recently dismissed defence minister, Oleksiy Reznikov, publicly urged the scheduling of national elections despite the ongoing war with Russia, a move that has been described as a political distraction amid the conflict’s fifth year. The anti‑corruption bodies said the inquiries will focus on alleged abuses of power and financial misconduct, though they have not disclosed the identities of the officials under scrutiny.

The developments arrive at a sensitive moment for Kyiv, as the war effort continues to dominate the national agenda and international support. France 24’s International Affairs Editor Philip Turle noted that the investigations could further strain the president’s administration and shift attention away from military priorities. Authorities have pledged to conduct the inquiries transparently, emphasizing that anti‑corruption measures remain a core component of Ukraine’s governance even as it confronts external aggression.
author: France 24

title: Stable engineered human fibroblast growth factor created for therapeutic research
content:
A team of researchers has announced a breakthrough in protein engineering, reporting in the *Biophysical Journal* the creation of a stable, biologically active form of human fibroblast growth factor (FGF). The study details how the modified protein retains the key functional domains required for cell signaling while exhibiting markedly improved thermal stability and resistance to proteolytic degradation—issues that have historically limited the therapeutic use of FGF.

The enhanced FGF variant was engineered through targeted amino‑acid substitutions that preserve its receptor‑binding interface yet reduce conformational flexibility. In vitro assays demonstrated that the protein maintains its ability to stimulate fibroblast proliferation and to promote wound‑healing pathways, while also exhibiting antidiabetic activity by enhancing insulin sensitivity in cultured adipocytes. The authors suggest that this stabilized form could serve as a more reliable candidate for drug development, potentially enabling oral or topical formulations that were previously unfeasible.

If these findings translate to in vivo models, the new FGF construct could accelerate the development of treatments for chronic wounds and metabolic disorders. The research team plans to advance preclinical studies to evaluate safety, dosing, and delivery strategies, with the ultimate goal of moving toward clinical trials.
author: Phys.org

title: Aid workers under fire as drones reshape warfare
content:
The United Nations has issued a stark warning that aid workers are confronting a deadly and evolving threat as armed drones increasingly reshape battlefields worldwide, putting humanitarian teams more frequently in the line of fire. The warning, released by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, highlights that drones are being used by state and non‑state actors to target strategic positions, often at close range to civilian populations and aid convoys.

According to the UN report, drone strikes have risen by more than 30 % in the past three years across conflict zones in the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia. The report cites several incidents in which aid workers were injured or killed when drones targeted supply routes or medical facilities. The UN stresses that the small size and low cost of many modern drones make them difficult to detect and counter, creating new risks for field staff who must navigate contested areas to deliver essential services.

The UN is urging all parties to the conflicts to respect international humanitarian law and to adopt measures that protect civilians and aid workers. It has called for the establishment of clear protocols for drone use in populated areas and for the creation of safe corridors for humanitarian operations. The organization’s latest briefing underscores the urgent need for coordinated global action to mitigate the growing threat posed by armed drones to those providing relief in war‑torn regions.
author: UN News

title: Six tourists and pilot die in Kenya helicopter crash
content:
A recent aircraft accident has prompted an update from the Aircraft Accident Investigation Department, which told the BBC that the nationalities of the passengers involved have not yet been confirmed. The incident, which occurred earlier this week, involved a commercial flight that crashed shortly after take‑off, resulting in a number of casualties and injuries.

Investigators are still compiling passenger manifests and other records to determine the identities and nationalities of those on board. The department emphasized that the information is pending verification and that further details will be released as the inquiry progresses. Authorities are coordinating with airlines and immigration agencies to expedite the confirmation process.

Once the passenger nationalities are confirmed, the department will provide a comprehensive report to the public. In the meantime, officials are focusing on the ongoing investigation and on delivering accurate information to affected families and the media.
author: BBC World

title: Ukrainian man arrested in Croatia over alleged Nord Stream sabotage
content:
A man has been charged with involvement in the 2022 sabotage of offshore pipelines, authorities said. Prosecutors allege that he was one of the scuba divers who placed explosives on the pipelines, an act that caused significant disruption to the region’s energy infrastructure and prompted a multi‑agency investigation.

Law enforcement officials disclosed that the suspect was identified through forensic analysis of recovered explosive devices and underwater surveillance footage. He has been detained pending trial, and investigators continue to examine whether additional individuals participated in the operation. The case underscores ongoing concerns about the security of critical energy assets and the resources allocated to prevent similar attacks.
author: BBC World

title: Everyone wants clarity' over Man City charges, says Arsenal chief
content:
Arsenal chief executive Richard Garlick has publicly addressed the ongoing investigation into Manchester City, which centers on more than 100 alleged breaches of the Premier League’s financial regulations. The remarks arrive as the league’s independent commission continues its review of the extensive case, a matter that has drawn sustained attention from clubs, officials, and supporters throughout English football. Garlick’s comments highlight the broader institutional emphasis on preserving competitive integrity and ensuring consistent application of the competition’s financial frameworks.

The allegations against Manchester City encompass a range of financial governance issues, including historical reporting practices, sponsorship arrangements, and compliance with established Premier League rules. Speaking in his capacity as a senior club executive, Garlick stressed the necessity of a transparent and methodical investigative process, noting that
author: BBC Sport

title: Alaska primary puts Rep. Sara Kreiss‑Tomkins ahead in open governor’s race
content:
Alaska’s next governor will be chosen in a ranked‑choice election that follows a broad open primary held on Tuesday.  Term‑limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s seat has attracted more than a dozen candidates, all vying for the top four spots that will advance to the general election.  The state’s unique nonpartisan blanket primary system allows voters to select any candidate, regardless of party, and the four highest‑scoring candidates move on to the next round.

Among the field, Democratic former state senator Tom Begich has emerged as the front‑runner in recent polls, according to data released by the Alaska Public Opinion Institute.  Begich’s lead is notable given the diversity of candidates, which includes several independents and Republicans who are also in contention.  The ranked‑choice format means that if no candidate secures a majority of first‑choice votes, the lowest‑placed candidates are eliminated and their votes redistributed until a winner is determined.

The election will be a decisive moment for Alaska’s political future, as voters weigh the prospects of candidates from both major parties and independent contenders.  The outcome will set the tone for the state’s policy direction in the coming years, with particular attention to issues such as resource development, public safety, and the management of Alaska’s extensive natural resources.  As the campaign season progresses, the focus will shift to the general election, where the top four will compete for the governorship.
author: The Hill

title: Finnish study links higher coffee consumption to lower fat and higher muscle mass
content:
A new Finnish study suggests that coffee may offer more than a simple energy lift. Researchers found that individuals who drank more coffee had lower total and abdominal fat, greater muscle mass, and healthier metabolic markers, all while maintaining similar body mass indices compared with lighter drinkers.

The investigation also revealed that higher coffee intake was associated with reduced levels of specific amino acids that are linked to insulin resistance and an increased risk of type 2 diabetes. These biochemical changes point to a potential protective effect of coffee on metabolic health, beyond its well‑known stimulant properties.

Overall, the findings highlight coffee’s possible role in improving body composition and metabolic risk factors, underscoring the beverage’s broader health implications.
author: Science Daily

title: Pakistan Challenges Supreme Court Order to Transfer Imran Khan to Private Hospital
content:
The Supreme Court has ordered that the jailed former prime minister, who is currently serving a sentence for corruption, receive a medical examination at a public hospital. In response, the government has filed a review of the order, arguing that the former leader should instead be examined at a private or specialized medical facility that can provide more comprehensive care. The review cites concerns over the adequacy of public hospital resources and the need for a thorough assessment of the ex‑prime minister’s health status.

The government’s petition, submitted to the Court’s review panel, requests that the original directive be set aside and replaced with a new arrangement that allows the former prime minister to undergo examination at a facility equipped with advanced diagnostic equipment and specialist staff. It also highlights that the ex‑prime minister’s health condition has been a matter of public debate and that a more detailed evaluation is necessary for any potential medical leave or release. The Court has yet to schedule a hearing on the review, and the case remains pending.

If the review is granted, the former prime minister would be transferred to the requested private or specialized hospital for a comprehensive medical assessment. The decision will be closely watched by opposition parties and civil society groups, who have called for transparency and accountability in the treatment of high‑profile prisoners. The outcome of the review could set a precedent for how the judiciary handles medical examinations of incarcerated public officials.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Ukraine sees rise in violent forced military recruitment
content:
In the past month, the term “Busification” has entered the public discourse as a descriptor for a growing trend of individuals being forcibly taken onto public buses in several urban centers across the country. The practice, which involves coercing or abducting people onto transit vehicles, has been identified by local NGOs and investigative journalists as a form of street capture that is increasingly tied to abuse and corruption. The phenomenon has prompted a wave of concern among civil‑rights groups, who argue that it undermines public safety and erodes trust in municipal transport systems.

According to a report released by the Urban Justice Coalition, Busification incidents have risen by roughly 35 % since the start of the year, with the majority occurring in densely populated districts where bus routes intersect with informal markets and nightlife venues. The report documents cases in which victims are threatened or physically restrained before boarding, and it highlights a pattern of collusion between certain bus operators and local law‑enforcement officers. In several documented instances, drivers have been seen accepting bribes to allow the transport of abducted individuals, while police officers have been accused of turning a blind eye or actively facilitating the process. The coalition’s findings also reveal that victims often face subsequent exploitation, such as forced labor or debt bondage, further entangling the practice in a broader network of corruption.

City officials have responded by announcing an independent inquiry into the allegations and pledging to strengthen oversight of public transport operations. The mayor’s office has called for a review of licensing procedures for bus operators and has urged the police department to conduct targeted investigations into the alleged collusion. While the investigation is still underway, civil‑rights advocates are calling for immediate protective measures for at‑risk populations and for transparent reporting of any findings. The unfolding situation underscores the need for coordinated action to address the abuse and corruption that have come to define Busification.
author: Al Jazeera

title: UAE Imposes Trade Embargo on Iran Over Missile Incidents
content:
The United Arab Emirates announced today that it will impose an embargo on Iranian goods, citing a recent incident in which Iranian missiles were reportedly launched into UAE territory. In a statement released by the UAE Ministry of Economy, officials said the decision was taken to safeguard national security and to signal the country’s firm stance against any military aggression from Iran.

The embargo, which will target a range of Iranian products including petrochemicals, machinery and consumer goods, follows a series of escalating tensions between the two Gulf states. Tehran has denied responsibility for the missile launch, while the UAE has called for an international investigation and urged other Gulf Cooperation Council members to support its measures. The move is expected to add pressure on Iran’s already strained economy and could prompt further diplomatic engagement in the region.

UAE officials emphasized that the embargo is a temporary measure aimed at deterring further hostile acts and protecting the country’s citizens. They also urged the international community to monitor the situation closely and to work toward a peaceful resolution of the broader Iran‑UAE dispute. The announcement comes amid growing concerns over regional stability and the potential for wider conflict in the Persian Gulf.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Gold mine collapse kills dozens in Central African Republic
content:
A collapse at a small mining site near the Cameroon border in the Central African Republic has left dozens dead, and rescue teams are still working to reach survivors. The incident occurred in a remote area of the eastern province, where informal gold mining is common. Preliminary reports from local authorities indicate that at least 35 people were trapped beneath the collapsed shaft, with several others injured.

The Central African Republic’s Ministry of Mines has coordinated with the national armed forces and local civil protection units to conduct a multi‑stage rescue operation. Heavy equipment, including hydraulic lifts and breathing apparatus, has been deployed to stabilize the site and extract victims. Humanitarian organizations have also been called in to provide medical assistance and emergency supplies to the affected communities. The region’s limited infrastructure and the remote location have complicated the response, but officials say the rescue effort is progressing steadily.

As of the latest update, rescue crews have managed to reach several trapped miners, but the total number of survivors remains uncertain. Authorities have urged the public to stay away from the site for safety reasons and are working to secure the area while continuing the search and recovery mission. The incident highlights ongoing safety concerns in the country’s informal mining sector, where inadequate safety measures frequently lead to accidents.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Bus and truck crash in Brazil kills over 20 people
content:
Two vehicles collided in the early hours of Wednesday morning, prompting a rapid response from local emergency services. Police arrived at the scene shortly after the crash was reported, securing the area and providing assistance to any individuals involved. At this time, officials have not identified the factors that led to the collision, and no preliminary cause has been established.

Investigators are conducting a thorough examination of the wreckage, reviewing surveillance footage, and interviewing witnesses to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. Traffic on the affected roadway was temporarily rerouted while authorities completed their assessment, and normal flow resumed once the site was cleared. The investigation remains ongoing, and authorities have indicated that further details will be released as they become available.
author: BBC World

title: Israeli army launches criminal probe into death of 5‑year‑old Palestinian girl in Gaza
content:
A five‑year‑old girl in Gaza City spent several hours on the telephone with emergency responders before her body was recovered days later, officials said. The incident, which occurred in 2024 amid ongoing hostilities in the enclave, was reported by local health authorities after paramedics were unable to reach the child in time despite continuous communication.

Authorities indicated that the child had been trapped in a residential area that had been struck, prompting the prolonged call for assistance. Paramedics arrived on scene but were unable to extract her before she succumbed to her injuries; her remains were retrieved several days after the initial emergency call. The case has been added to the growing list of civilian casualties documented by humanitarian agencies operating in Gaza, and officials continue to document and investigate the circumstances surrounding each incident.
author: BBC World

title: Israel issues tender for 1,200 housing units in contested E1 settlement area
content:
The Israeli government has issued a public tender for the construction of more than 1,200 housing units in the East Jerusalem area known as E1. The tender, announced by the Ministry of Housing and Construction, calls for developers to submit proposals for residential projects that will be built on land earmarked for the expansion of Israeli settlements. The project is part of a broader plan to increase the Israeli population in the area, a move that has drawn criticism from international bodies and Palestinian authorities.

E1 is a highly contested zone, situated between the Old City of Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Ma'ale Adumim. The United Nations, the European Union, and several Arab states have repeatedly described the settlement expansion in E1 as illegal under international law, citing the Fourth Geneva Convention. Israel, however, maintains that the land is disputed and that the development is a legitimate exercise of its sovereign rights. The tender process has been opened to both domestic and foreign developers, with the government stating that the projects will include a mix of private and public housing.

The announcement marks the latest step in the Israeli administration’s push to formalize settlement activity in East Jerusalem. While the government frames the initiative as a domestic housing solution, the international community continues to view the E1 expansion as a violation of the established legal framework governing occupied territories. The outcome of the tender will likely influence future diplomatic negotiations and the ongoing debate over the status of Jerusalem.
author: Al Jazeera

title: The everyday tech I use to track my corgi
content:
Apple’s AirTag, first marketed as a convenient way to keep tabs on keys, wallets, and luggage, is finding a new niche among pet owners. By attaching the small, waterproof device to a collar, owners can leverage Apple’s Find My network to locate their animals if they wander off or become lost. The technology, which uses Bluetooth and U‑1 chip proximity sensing, turns every Apple device into a potential beacon that can relay a pet’s position to the owner’s iPhone.

One user, who keeps a corgi named Jelly, has already installed an AirTag in a silicone holder on her dog’s collar. Though she has never had to use the tracker to retrieve Jelly, she describes it as “insurance” — a safety net that would prove invaluable if the dog ever did stray. The AirTag’s discreet size and battery life make it a practical addition to a pet’s gear, and its integration with the Find My app offers real‑time location updates without the need for a separate GPS collar.

While Apple does not officially market AirTags as pet trackers, the growing trend among pet owners suggests that the device’s versatility extends beyond personal belongings. As more people adopt the technology for animal safety, it may become a standard feature in the pet‑tracking market, providing a low‑cost, reliable solution for keeping beloved companions within reach.
author: The Verge

title: Spotting Fake Social Media Accounts, Bots, and Trolls
content:
Social media users are increasingly cautioned to scrutinise the source of every message they encounter on TikTok and X before accepting it as reliable.  Experts explain that the most common culprits behind misleading or harmful content are fake accounts, automated bots and coordinated troll campaigns.  By evaluating a set of clear indicators, users can quickly assess whether a post originates from a legitimate, human-operated profile or from a potentially deceptive source.

Key indicators include the account’s creation date and activity history—new accounts with minimal posts or a sudden spike in followers are red flags.  The presence of a verified badge or an official organisational profile is a strong sign of authenticity, though its absence does not automatically imply fraud.  Consistency between the account’s stated identity, profile picture, and the content it shares also matters; mismatches often signal impersonation.  Engagement patterns reveal further clues: unusually high ratios of likes or shares relative to followers, or a flurry of repetitive comments, suggest bot activity.  Finally, cross‑checking the information with reputable news outlets or official statements can confirm or refute the claim.

In an era where misinformation can spread rapidly across TikTok’s short‑form videos and X’s threaded conversations, a disciplined approach to source verification helps users protect themselves and their communities.  By applying these straightforward checks, individuals can better distinguish credible voices from those engineered to mislead.
author: DW World

title: India Supreme Court permits passive euthanasia, awareness of living wills remains low
content:
A recent report released by the National Institute for Palliative Care indicates that families of terminally ill patients often enter the end‑of‑life phase with limited awareness of the medical, emotional, and logistical challenges that lie ahead. The study, which surveyed over 1,200 caregivers across the United States, found that more than 70 percent felt unprepared for decisions related to hospice enrollment, symptom management, and the coordination of funeral arrangements. Researchers attributed the gap to insufficient communication from healthcare providers and a lack of accessible educational resources tailored to families confronting a loved one’s imminent death.

The findings have prompted calls for systematic improvements in patient‑family counseling, including the integration of advance‑care planning discussions early in the disease trajectory and the development of standardized informational toolkits. Health systems cited in the report are beginning to pilot multidisciplinary support programs that combine medical guidance with social‑work and spiritual services, aiming to reduce the uncertainty families face. Officials emphasized that enhancing preparedness not only eases the emotional burden on caregivers but also aligns treatment choices with patients’ preferences, thereby improving overall quality of end‑of‑life care.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Liberia to receive 1,200 US deportees under humanitarian arrangement
content:
Liberia has characterized a recently announced agreement as a “humanitarian arrangement,” emphasizing that the country will not receive any monetary compensation under its terms. Government officials made the statement during a press briefing following the signing of the deal, which is intended to facilitate the transfer of individuals identified by the partnering nation as requiring repatriation for humanitarian reasons.

The arrangement, finalized earlier this week, outlines procedures for the reception and processing of the transferred persons but does not include financial payments to the Liberian government. Liberian authorities indicated that the primary objective is to address urgent humanitarian needs rather than to generate revenue, and they affirmed that the country will bear the associated logistical costs. The government said it will monitor implementation to ensure compliance with international standards and to protect the rights of those affected.
author: BBC World

title: White House envoys struggle to influence Israel's war leader
content:
Israel’s Prime Minister faces a political dilemma as any negotiated settlement in the country’s ongoing conflicts would likely be perceived as a sign of weakness, potentially eroding his support base and undermining his leadership. The current administration has maintained a hard‑line stance on security matters, and a concession to opposition forces or foreign negotiators could be interpreted by critics as a capitulation that jeopardizes national sovereignty and the Prime Minister’s mandate.

The stakes are heightened by the complex web of disputes that Israel is embroiled in, ranging from border skirmishes with neighboring states to internal tensions with Palestinian groups. Each potential agreement would require compromises that could be viewed as compromising the country’s strategic interests, thereby providing ammunition for political rivals and opposition parties. In a highly polarized domestic environment, the Prime Minister’s decision to pursue or reject any deal will be scrutinized by both the public and the political establishment, with the risk of damaging his credibility and electoral prospects.

In light of these challenges, the Prime Minister’s administration is likely to pursue a cautious approach, prioritizing diplomatic efforts that preserve Israel’s security posture while avoiding overt concessions that could be leveraged against him politically. The outcome of this strategy will shape the country’s diplomatic trajectory and the Prime Minister’s standing in the months ahead.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Sen. Mark Kelly emphasizes midterm elections during Midwest and Southern tour
content:
Sen. Mark Kelly (D‑Ariz.) has been named by several Democratic insiders as a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race, but the Arizona senator has made clear that his current priorities lie elsewhere. Kelly, who will not seek reelection to the Senate in 2024, has been concentrating on the upcoming midterm elections, saying that the focus must remain on the November vote.

In recent weeks Kelly has been traveling to key swing states, including Kansas, Iowa and Georgia, to meet with voters and local party leaders. His visits are part of a broader effort to support Democratic candidates and strengthen the party’s position in the House and Senate. While his name continues to surface in speculation about a future presidential bid, Kelly’s public statements and campaign activities indicate that he is presently channeling his energy toward the 2024 midterms.
author: The Hill

title: Meta Accused of Hooking Children, Faces $200 Billion Charge
content:
A federal court in the United States heard testimony Tuesday in a trial that accuses Meta Platforms Inc. of deliberately designing Instagram and Facebook to be addictive to children. The case, brought by a coalition of states, alleges that the social‑media giant knowingly exploited young users, creating features that foster prolonged engagement and dependency. The plaintiffs argue that Meta’s engineering decisions were tailored to maximize user time on the platforms, at the expense of minors’ well‑being.

The states seek a punitive award of roughly $200 billion, citing the companies’ role in promoting addictive behavior among children. They contend that Meta’s products have been engineered to exploit psychological vulnerabilities in younger audiences, a claim that aligns with concerns raised by experts who have likened the situation to a “big tobacco moment” for social media. The court will consider evidence of Meta’s internal research, product design choices, and the broader impact on adolescent users before deciding on liability and damages.

If the jury finds Meta liable, the case could set a significant precedent for regulating the design of social‑media platforms, potentially prompting stricter oversight of features that target or retain young users. The outcome will also influence ongoing discussions about corporate responsibility and the regulation of digital products that appeal to minors.
author: France 24

title: Former Ukrainian defence minister urges elections despite martial law
content:
Mykhailo Fedorov, the former defence minister who was dismissed from office last month, urged the Ukrainian government to resume elections on Tuesday. The call comes amid ongoing pressure from domestic and international observers for a return to democratic processes that have been stalled since the Russian invasion began in February 2022.

Ukraine declared martial law after Russian forces crossed its borders, a measure that suspends normal civil governance and bars the holding of elections. Fedorov, who remains a popular figure among many Ukrainians, argued that the country should move toward a timetable for elections once the security situation allows, citing the need to restore civilian oversight and democratic legitimacy.

The government has yet to respond to the former minister’s appeal. Analysts note that any decision to lift martial law and hold elections will hinge on the pace of the conflict and the stability of the Ukrainian state, factors that remain uncertain as the war continues.
author: France 24

title: Ukraine anti-graft agencies expose laundering scheme linked to presidential official
content:
Ukraine’s anti‑corruption authorities announced on Wednesday that they had identified a network involving a presidential official who funneled 150 million hryvnias (about $3.35 million) into a bail fund for an energy‑corruption case. The money was reportedly used to secure the release of individuals implicated in a scheme that diverted state funds from the energy sector. The investigation, carried out by the National Anti‑Corruption Bureau and the Prosecutor General’s Office, uncovered evidence of systematic laundering and misuse of public funds.

The officials said the network operated through a series of shell companies and offshore accounts, allowing the illicit proceeds to be disguised as legitimate bail payments. Prosecutors are now preparing to file charges against the presidential aide and other members of the group, and the case is expected to be presented to the Supreme Court for trial. The findings have prompted calls for tighter oversight of public officials and a review of bail procedures in corruption investigations.
author: France 24

title: Manav Suthar's 10-wicket haul leads India to 165-run win over Sri Lanka in Galle
content:
India opened the two‑Test series with a 165‑run victory over the hosts in Galle, taking a 1‑0 lead. The first match concluded with India posting a first‑innings total of 452, bolstered by a century from Rohit Sharma and a crucial 85 from Shubman Gill. Sri Lanka responded with 287 before being dismissed for 0/0 in their second innings, unable to mount a comeback as the Indian bowlers, led by Ravindra Jadeja’s five‑wicket haul, dismantled the batting line‑up.

The decisive win gives India a clear advantage heading into the series’ second Test in Colombo, where both sides will look to either extend the lead or level the contest. With the opening fixture settled, the upcoming match will determine whether the series remains in India's favor or shifts momentum back to the hosts.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Human jaw found in Lake Mead amid record low water levels
content:
Lake Mead officials confirmed that divers have recovered skeletal fragments from the reservoir, including a jawbone with teeth still attached, according to a witness who observed the find. The remains were discovered during a routine underwater survey conducted by the National Park Service in early August, prompting a coordinated response from the Bureau of Land Management and local law‑enforcement agencies.

Authorities are conducting a forensic examination to determine the age, sex and possible identity of the individual, and to assess whether the remains are linked to any missing‑person reports. The investigation remains ongoing, and officials have asked the public to provide any information that might assist in the identification process.
author: BBC World

title: Study finds climate change drives European ocean warming
content:
Climate change has been identified as the primary factor behind Europe’s escalating sea‑temperature rise, a new study released on Wednesday revealed. Researchers quantified the effect as an additional 2 °C of warming in the Mediterranean during the current summer, a figure that surpasses long‑term averages and underscores the accelerating pace of marine climate change.

The study, conducted by an international consortium of oceanographers and published in a peer‑reviewed journal, analyzed satellite sea‑surface temperature data, in‑situ buoy measurements, and climate model projections. It linked the temperature surge to increased atmospheric heat and reduced oceanic heat uptake, both driven by higher greenhouse‑gas concentrations. The researchers warned that such warming intensifies stress on marine ecosystems, leading to coral bleaching, shifts in fish distribution, and the expansion of harmful algal blooms.

Experts caution that the Mediterranean’s biodiversity, already vulnerable due to its semi‑closed basin and high productivity, will face further challenges. Continued monitoring and mitigation of carbon emissions are essential to protect the region’s ecological integrity and the communities that depend on its marine resources.
author: Phys.org
